records.c: The NMI handler. CIA 2's timers A and B, started at fixed raster lines by start_split_timers, interrupt twice a frame: timer A puts the playfield's fine scroll (scroll_x) and multicolour into $D016 and turns extended colour off; timer B turns extended colour on with no scroll for the power-up bar. Saves only A.
Tests sprite collisions (check_collisions), then reads the keyboard for pause: with P down it enters pause, otherwise it updates the power-up bar.
Sets all three voices' pitch from the first sprite's height, then plays a sound and moves on. Called while the ship explodes.
Calls the sound routine at $9BE1 and continues at $7623.

Pause, entered with interrupts off: keeps the screen split by watching the raster (line 74 for the playfield, 228 for the bar) and keeps the music and the bar going, until P is pressed again; then waits for P to be let go.
Jumps to play_frame_tail.
If P is down, turns the raster interrupt off, waits for P to be let go, runs pause_loop, and turns the interrupt back on.
Lights the power-up bar's current choice: resets the six boxes to colour 11, then paints the five cells of the chosen box in a colour from bar_flash, which cycles each call.
Eight colours the chosen power-up box cycles through.
Counter that steps through bar_flash.
Paints the six power-up boxes colour 11 and loads X with the current choice (powerup_pos).
Set to 1 by title_keys when fire or RETURN is down; the attract loop starts a game on it.
How many passes in a row SPACE has been down on the title, stopping at 2; the attract loop steps the player count when it reaches 1.
Which player (0 to 4) game_loop is running.
Set to 1 by game_loop when the player it just ran still has lives, so the round of turns goes again.
Character codes of the logo's top row.
Character codes of the logo's bottom row.
Copies the two rows of the GRADIUS logo (17 characters each) to the screen at rows 6 and 7 in colour 9.

The game's first instruction, where the second unpacker hands over. Waits about 150 frames (wait_frames), turns the screen on (screen_on), clears the screen and sets up stage 0 (stage_setup), clears it again, sets two colours, turns every sprite off and copies the title's characters in (title_charset). Then the attract loop: draws the PLAYER GAME line and the title text, waits for raster line 255, moves the star field (title_stars) and reads the keys (title_keys). Fire or RETURN starts a game with the chosen number of players; SPACE, held for three passes, steps the count from one to four.
Number of players for the next game, 1 to 4, stepped by SPACE on the title (title_next_count) and shown by title_player_line.
Offset of each player's 10-digit score in score_store ($0200): 0, 10, 20, 30, 40.
Zeroes the 50 bytes at $0200-$0231 that hold five 10-digit scores, one per player slot.

One whole game. Gives every player three lives and the stage they last reached, then takes the players in turn: copies a player's score into the live score digits at $4000, sets the stage, runs the stage's play (stage_play, from $173A), and on return turns sprites and sound off. A player out of lives gets GAME OVER (game_over_text) and the high-score check; the others keep their score and stage. When nobody has lives left it reads RETURN once: held, a new game starts at once with three lives each; otherwise back to the title.
The words ONE, TWO, THREE and FOUR, eight ASCII bytes each, for the title and the PLAYER line.
Letters in each of ONE, TWO, THREE and FOUR.
" PLAYER GAME", ASCII padded with spaces, printed after the player count on the title.
Which of ONE to FOUR print_player_word prints (1 to 4).
Offset of that word in player_words.
Letters left to print.
Prints ONE, TWO, THREE or FOUR (word_number) at screen row 11 plus Y, in colour 9. Letters are ASCII, turned into screen codes by adding $40.
Prints the player count and " PLAYER GAME" on the title, row 11.
Steps player_count 1, 2, 3, 4, 1.
Reads the title's inputs: RETURN or fire on port 2 sets start_pressed; SPACE counts up space_held, which clears when it is let go.

Clears the screen and resets the stage (through $FE00), then prints "PLAYER " and the player's number word, as shown before each turn. Its third byte is followed by $FB $B0 $41, which the processor runs as ISC $41B0,Y (an undocumented instruction that adds one to a byte and subtracts it from A) where JSR $41B0 seems meant.
"GAME OVER" in ASCII.
Prints GAME OVER at the middle of the screen, in colour 9.
Waits for raster line 255 to come round 150 times, about three seconds on a PAL machine.
Loads stage 5's character set into $3C00 (load_stage_charset with stage 5) for the title, and puts the stage number back.
The stage each player starts on, copied to every player when a game begins.
The score of the player now playing, ten decimal digits from the most significant, one per byte. game_loop copies each player's ten digits in and out of score_store at $0200 around a turn.
Finds the first non-zero digit of the score and carries on at $FF00, which prints it.
Adds one to the eighth score digit, which is the hundreds, carrying up through the digits to the second (the carry never reaches the first).
Adds A hundreds to the score, one at a time through add_100. Keeps X and Y.
Holds X across add_points.
Holds Y across add_points.
Sprite table, low byte of X, one per slot 0 to 7. Slot 0 is the Vic Viper. The tables that follow are indexed the same way and copied to the video chip each frame by draw_sprites.
Sprite table, Y position of each slot.
Sprite table, ninth bit of X, 0 or 1.
Sprite table, each slot's colour.
Sprite table, non-zero to draw the slot at double width and height.
Sprite table, non-zero to draw the slot in multicolour.
Sprite table, the shape's first pointer value; spr_anim is added to it.
Sprite table, the animation step added to spr_frame.
Sprite table, non-zero when the slot is in use.

Rebuilds the video chip's sprites from the sprite tables: clears enables, ninth bits, expansion and multicolour, then hands each slot that is on to draw_sprite. Slots in use take the hardware sprites in order, so a gap in the tables leaves no gap in the hardware.
Puts sprite table slot X into the next free hardware sprite: position, enable bit, ninth X bit, expansion, multicolour, colour, and the shape pointer at $07F8 (spr_frame plus spr_anim).
The eight bit masks $01 to $80, one per sprite.
Twice the number of hardware sprites draw_sprites has filled, the offset into $D000.
The Vic Viper's X, low byte.
The Vic Viper's X, ninth bit.
The Vic Viper's Y.
Set to 1 when the Vic Viper is hit, by a sprite collision (check_collisions) or by the scenery at $56DA; the play loop reads it each pass.
Frames until launch_fans sends the next formation.
Set when the explosion about to start should leave a capsule behind.
Low byte of the screen address of each of the 25 rows.
High byte of the screen address of each row ($04 to $07).
Points $FB/$FC at the screen cell in column cell_x of row cell_y, using the row-address tables at $415C and $4176. Keeps X; returns Y = 0.
Holds X across screen_addr.
Column for screen_addr.
Row for screen_addr.
Fills screen memory $0400-$07FF with spaces ($20). Ends with Y = 0.
One colour per screen row, painted into colour RAM by stage_setup; loaded per stage.
The power-up bar's 37 character codes as drawn along screen row 24: the words SPEEDUP, MISSILE, DOUBLE, LASER, MULTI and ? in the bar's own letters ($80 up), with $24 between boxes.
A second copy of the bar's character codes, the same layout.
The column at which each of the six power-up boxes starts on row 24.
Which power-up box is lit, 0 to 5, or $FF for none. Each capsule the Vic Viper picks up moves it one box on.
Redraws the power-up bar on row 24: copies bar_text to the screen and colours every cell black except the $73 cells, then paints the lit box (powerup_pos) red.
Each shot's screen column.
The Vic Viper's character shots, nine slots: each one's screen row; 0 when free. Slots 0-5 take ordinary shots, 6-8 the DOUBLE shots.

Returns a pseudo-random number from 0 to A-1 in A. Mixes a running sum, a counter, the joystick port, a seed byte and a byte of the table at $A000, then takes it modulo A by repeated subtraction. Keeps X.
Every third call, takes one of twelve background stars at random, erases it if it is still a star character ($4B), and puts it at a new random cell.
Thrown objects, X low byte, eight slots.
Thrown objects, Y; 0 for a free slot.
Thrown objects, X ninth bit.
Thrown objects, upward speed, taken from Y each frame; negative values fall.
Thrown objects, sideways speed.
Thrown objects, the sprite slot each rides.
Thrown objects, 1 to move right, 0 to move left.
Thrown objects, frames left before the upward speed drops by one.

Moves up to eight thrown objects, each riding a sprite slot: X goes left or right by its speed, Y climbs by a speed that falls by one every four frames, so each flies in an arc. One that leaves rows $52-$DB is switched off with its sprite.

Starts a thrown object if a sprite slot (1 to 6) and an object slot are free: a random direction, sideways speed 0-3 and upward speed 3-7, from Y $B0 and one of two X positions, with one of three random shapes and colours; plays sound 6. In the stages that erupt, these are the volcanoes' rocks.
The two X positions (less 16) that thrown objects start from.
The three colours a thrown object can take.
Code that nothing calls: a loop that sets up the Big Core (core_setup) and runs its movement, lasers and sprites once a frame, as if to test it on its own.
X of each of the six sprites that make up the Big Core, three across and two down.
Y of each of the six.
Shape of each of the six.

Builds the Big Core, the end-of-stage boss: resets its core walls (core_walls_reset) and the dissolve (dissolve_reset), then puts its six parts in sprite slots 1 to 6, doubled in size, blue, at the right of the screen, and sets it entering.
The Big Core's state: 1 while it slides in from the right, 3 once in place and moving up and down.
Each frame of the Big Core: runs the dissolve, then in state 1 slides all six parts left a pixel until they reach X $126, then switches to state 3; in state 3 moves them up and down (core_bob).
Frames left before the Big Core next chooses which way to move.
Counts the Big Core's turns; it moves only on odd counts.
The Big Core's vertical step: 1 down, -1 up.

The Big Core's vertical movement: every 16 frames turns toward the Vic Viper (down while the ship is lower than the core), then on odd turns moves its six parts a pixel, staying between Y $4C and $8C.
The four core lasers' columns.
The four core lasers' rows; 0 when off.
How far right of column 22 each laser starts.
How far below the core's row each laser starts.
Frames until the Big Core fires again.

The Big Core's four lasers, drawn in characters: every 60 frames, once the core is in place, starts four three-character beams level with it; each frame moves each beam a column left, erasing its old cells, until it reaches the left edge.
The shapes of the Big Core's walls at each stage of damage, eight bytes a stage, written into its sprite shapes at $29F9 and $2A80.
How many of the Big Core's walls have been shot away, 0 to 5; $FF when no core is on screen.
Sets core_hits to 0 and draws the walls whole.
Writes the wall shape for the current damage into the core's two sprite shapes.
A shot reached the core: adds one to core_hits, plays sound 4 and redraws the walls; at 5 the core is destroyed.
Starts the dissolve at the first character and the first pixel pair.
Which of the four two-bit pixel positions the dissolve is clearing.
The address the dissolve works on, in the characters from $3C00 to $3CFF.
Which of eight rows (in a scattered order) the dissolve is clearing in each character.

One step of the dissolve that wipes the background as the Big Core arrives: clears one pixel pair in one row of one character at $3C00-$3CFF, moving eight bytes on each call. After the four pixel positions of every row the characters are blank, and the stage's rows are cleared from the screen (clear_rows).
The four two-pixel masks the dissolve clears, in turn.
The mask that keeps the other pixels.
The order in which the dissolve takes the eight rows of a character.
Runs dissolve_step 20 times; called once a frame.
0 while the dissolve runs, 2 when it has just finished, 1 when the rows are cleared.
Blanks the seven screen rows listed in rows_to_clear: the top row of play and the six above the bar.
The rows clear_rows blanks: 3 and 15 to 21.
The sprite slot of each of three homing enemies, $FF when the slot is free.
The rows (Y) the three homing enemies start at.
The X positions (above 256) they start at.
Starts a group of three homing enemies at the right edge, in the colour given in A, each in the next free sprite slot from 1 to 6, with shape $8E.
Colour for the enemies a spawn routine starts.
Which of the three homing enemies may steer this time; moves to the next every 12 frames.
Frames left before homer_turn moves on.

Moves the three homing enemies two pixels left a frame; the one whose turn it is also climbs or dives two pixels toward the Vic Viper's height, with a shape that leans up ($8F) or down ($90). One that leaves at the left, is switched off, or has become an explosion (shape $95) frees its slot.
22 heights of a sine-like wave, 0 to 30, that the wave enemies add to their starting row.
The shape each wave enemy shows at each point of the wave, $91 to $94.
Where each of the two wave enemies is in the wave, counted in half steps up to 44.
The rows the two wave enemies start at.
The sprite slot of each of the two wave enemies, $FF when free.
Starts two wave enemies at the right edge (X $158), in the colour given in A.
Moves the two wave enemies two pixels left a frame while they rise and fall through the wave, changing shape with it; frees one that leaves at the left or has been shot.
Keeps Y while move_wavers reads the wave.
Hopping enemies (four slots), Y; 0 when the slot is free.
Hopping enemies, X low byte.
Hopping enemies, X ninth bit.
Hopping enemies, sideways step each frame: 4 to the right, or $FB (five to the left).
Hopping enemies, upward speed, taken from Y each frame and reduced by one every five frames, so they fall back.
Hopping enemies, an animation counter; its bits pick shapes $A0 to $A3.
Hopping enemies, frames left before the upward speed drops.
Hopping enemies, the sprite slot each rides.

Moves the four hopping enemies: each flies in an arc under its falling speed, and when it lands on scenery (a character $80 or above under it) bounces up with speed 5, plays sound 7, and turns to hop toward the Vic Viper's column. One that rises above row $52 has its speed reversed. One that leaves at either side, or whose sprite has been switched off, is freed.
The Vic Viper's screen column, worked out from its X at the start of move_hoppers.
Walking enemies (two slots), X.
Walking enemies, Y; 0 when free.
Walking enemies, 0 while walking right along the scenery, $FA once it has reached the right side and walks left with the scroll.
Walking enemies, the shape, $9B to $9D as it walks; $9E when it stops.

Moves the two walking enemies along the ground or the ceiling: each steps two pixels right with a three-frame walk, follows the scenery up or down a character to stay on its surface, and turns back at X $F8. A walker in the top half of the screen (Y below $64) takes the upside-down shapes, $11 lower. Frees one whose sprite has gone.
Walking enemies, the sprite slot each rides.
Walking enemies, frames left before the next step of the walk.
The stage being played, 0 to 7.
Power-up capsules, up to ten (capsule_count of them are read): each one's row; 0 when free. A capsule is a block of four characters, $78-$7B.
Each capsule's column.
Each capsule's colour: 15 for an ordinary capsule, 14 for the blue one that clears the screen.
How many capsule slots are in use: 4.

Scrolls the playfield one character left: copies each of the 19 rows from 3 to 21, columns 1 to 39, one place to the left. The new right-hand column is drawn next frame (map_column). Colour RAM is not moved here; recolour_row and recolour_blocks keep it right.
Pixels the Vic Viper moves left or right each step; SPEEDUP raises it.
Pixels it moves up or down each step.
Reads joystick port 2 and moves the Vic Viper: up, down, right, left (ship_up and the rest), and fire (fire_button). Releasing fire clears fire_held.
Moves the Vic Viper up by ship_speed_y unless it is at the top (Y $4E); sets ship_moved and the tilt.
Which way the ship last moved vertically: $FF up, 1 down, 0 level; picks its banked shape.
Moves the Vic Viper down unless it is at the bottom (Y $CB).
Moves the Vic Viper right unless it is at the right edge (X $12C).
Moves the Vic Viper left unless it is at the left edge (X $38).
Frames before the Vic Viper can fire again.
Frames left in the hold that stops held fire from firing every frame; letting go clears it.
Fire is down: if both counters are clear, fires (fire_shot), sets both to 16 and plays sound 3; otherwise counts them down. Held, the ship fires every 17 frames.
The keyboard controls, read beside the joystick: Z left, X right, ; up, / down, RETURN fire, and right SHIFT to take the lit power-up (take_powerup).
Set when the Vic Viper moved this frame; the options then follow (options_follow).
One step of the player's controls: reads the joystick and the keys, copies the ship's position into sprite slot 0, sets its shape (ship_shape), and when it moved, records the move for the options.
Set when the ship moved right this frame.
Where the next column of the stage's map is read, low byte.
Where the next column of the stage's map is read, high byte.
Screen address (low byte) of the right-hand cell of each of the 19 playfield rows, 3 to 21.
Screen address (high byte) of the same cells.

Draws the stage's next column at the right edge of rows 3 to 21 from the map. The map is a stream of bytes: a value of $7F or more is a character to place in the next row; a smaller value is a count of empty rows to fill with spaces. When the 19 rows are filled the pointer moves past what it read.
Bytes of the map read for this column.
Spaces left to place for a run of empty rows.
Each shot's kind: 1 for an ordinary shot, which moves two columns a frame along its row; 2 for a DOUBLE shot, which moves one column right and one row up.

Moves the Vic Viper's shots, which are characters on the screen, not sprites. Each erases its old cell and moves on; it is drawn as character $29, or $28 for the rising DOUBLE shot. A shot that meets solid scenery (a character from $80 up to scenery_limit), passes column 38 or leaves rows 4 to 20 is freed, and one that hits scenery plays sound 7.
The first slot for each kind of shot: 0 for ordinary shots, 6 for DOUBLE shots.

Starts a shot of the kind in A (1 ordinary, 2 DOUBLE) at the position in cell_x, cell_y and the X high byte, in the first free slot of its kind. Ordinary shots may have twice shot_limit on screen, DOUBLE shots shot_limit. The pixel position becomes a cell: X over 8, less 3, and (Y - 42) over 8.
How many shots each emitter may have on screen: the number of emitters, the ship plus its options.
The number of slots start_shot may search for this kind of shot.
The kind of shot start_shot is placing.
The Vic Viper's five shapes, from banked hard down ($87) through level ($80) to banked hard up ($85).
Which of ship_shapes the ship shows, 0 to 4.
For each bank, the next one on the way back to level.
Frames until the bank changes again.
Every six frames tilts the Vic Viper one step toward its direction of travel (up or down), or back toward level when it is not moving vertically, and sets its shape in sprite slot 0.
Blanks the right-hand column of rows 3 to 21, in place of a map column when there is no scenery.
Set while the stage's map is being drawn; clear in open space, when the right-hand column is blanked instead.
Draws the next map column at the right edge (map_column), or a blank one when scenery_on is clear.
Set once the player has taken MISSILE: each shot also drops a missile.
Set once the player has taken DOUBLE: each shot also fires a rising shot.
Set once the player has taken LASER: shots are lasers instead of ordinary shots.
Code that nothing calls: copies the Vic Viper's position into cell_x, cell_y and the X high byte, the setup fire_from_point needs, as if from a version that fired only from the ship.
Fires from one point (cell_x, cell_y): a laser if the player has LASER, otherwise an ordinary shot; a DOUBLE shot as well if they have DOUBLE; and a missile if they have MISSILE.
Starts a laser at the point in cell_x and cell_y in the first free laser slot, up to shot_limit.
The character the laser being drawn uses.
Lasers, three slots: the column of each one's start.
Lasers, each one's Y as a pixel row less 40; 0 when free.

Moves the three lasers. Each erases its old span of laser_length cells (stopping at solid scenery, though character $96 does not stop it), moves three columns right, and draws the span again in colour 11 with the last cell in colour 9. The laser character is $5C plus the low three bits of its pixel row, so the beam sits at the ship's exact height inside the character. A laser that meets solid scenery or passes column 36 is freed.
Cells of the laser span still to erase or draw.

Takes the power-up whose box is lit (powerup_pos), as right SHIFT does from the keyboard. SPEEDUP adds one to both ship speeds, up to 4. MISSILE gives missiles, and a second MISSILE makes them move every frame instead of every other. DOUBLE gives the rising shot and takes LASER away; LASER gives lasers and takes DOUBLE away, each putting back the other's box. MULTI adds an option, up to two. ? gives the shield, four hits' worth. A power-up that can go no further has its box blanked (bar_blank), and once a box is blank, choosing it does nothing. Taking one turns the bar off, plays sound 1 and redraws the bar.
How many more hits the Vic Viper can take: set to 4 by the ? power-up; the play loop takes one off for each hit, and a collision with a big sprite empties it.
How many cells long a laser is: 5.
Fills one power-up box (five characters from offset X in bar_text) with character $23, so the word no longer shows.
Frames between missile steps: 2 after the first MISSILE, 1 after the second.
Frames left before the missiles next move.

Moves the missiles, which use shot slots 9 to 11 (rows at $4280, columns at $4274). Each erases its cell and moves one column right and one row down, as character $2A; where the cell below is solid it stays on its row instead, as character $29, so it runs along the ground. A missile that hits scenery (sound 7), leaves rows 3 to 20 or passes column 37 is freed.

Characters from $80 up to this value, less one, are solid scenery that stops the Vic Viper's shots, lasers and missiles; characters from here up are background they pass through. $AB on most stages, $F0 on the sixth (index 5). The ship itself collides with any character from $90 up (scenery_touch).
Starts a missile in the first free slot of 9 to 11, at the point start_shot is given.
The Vic Viper's last 16 positions, X low byte. The options follow seven and fourteen steps behind.
The same, X ninth bit.
The same, Y.
Index of the newest entry in the trail (low four bits).
Called when the ship moves: adds its position to the trail.
How many points fire at once: 1 for the ship, plus one for each option.
Index into the ship's trail of the point now firing.
Points still to fire this shot.
Fires a volley: from the Vic Viper's place in its trail and from each option's, seven steps further back each time, calls fire_from_point for every one.
The colour RAM address of the row recolour_row repaints next.
The row recolour_row repaints next.

Repaints one row of colour RAM a call, moving down rows 3 to 21 and back to 3: every cell that holds a space, a character below $80, or a character from scenery_limit up gets the row's colour from row_colours. The colours do not scroll with the characters, so this keeps the background and shots in their row's colour while solid scenery keeps the colours it was drawn with.
Keeps the colour RAM under each capsule right as the playfield scrolls: for a capsule within three rows of the row recolour_row is on, paints its four cells in its colour.
Points the JSR in new_column at the map drawer for this stage: map_column on every stage except the fourth (index 3), which has a drawer of its own at $54DF.
The playfield's background colour, written to $D021 by the interrupt; set to 1 (white) for a flash.

Moves each capsule one column left and draws it again: characters $78-$7B over two rows and two columns, the left pair in the capsule's colour and the right in the row's colour. One that reaches column 0 is erased (erase_capsule).
Blanks capsule X's four cells and frees the slot.
Counts capsules dropped; every seventh is the blue one.
Leaves a capsule at the cell in cell_x and cell_y, if it lies between columns 2 and 35 and a slot is free. Every seventh capsule dropped is blue (colour 14), the rest are ordinary (colour 15).
The colour of the capsule being dropped.
The nine cells round the Vic Viper that scenery_touch reads: three columns across and three rows down from its top-left cell.
1 for the cells of the middle row, where scenery is deadly; 0 for the rest, which only collect capsules.

Finds the Vic Viper's cell from its position and reads the nine cells round it. A character from $90 up in the middle row sets ship_hit. A capsule character in any of the nine collects that capsule (collect_capsule).
The four characters of a capsule, top left, top right, bottom left, bottom right.
How far each capsule character is from the capsule's left column.
How far each is from its top row.
Column offset of each of the nine cells scenery_touch reads.
Row offset of each.
The ship has touched a capsule character: works out the capsule's top-left cell from which character it touched, finds that capsule, erases it, gives its power (capsule_power) and scores 500.

An ordinary capsule moves the lit box of the power-up bar one on (from none to SPEEDUP, and from ? back round to SPEEDUP) and plays sound 0. The blue capsule destroys the enemies on screen instead (blue_capsule).
The colour of the capsule just collected.
Character-drawn formation enemies, twelve slots in two groups of six (0-5 and 6-11): each one's column.
Each one's row.
Each one's state: 0 free, 1 flying, 2 waiting to enter.
The formations' flight script: indices into fan_dx and fan_dy, one per leg, each script ending in $FF. Group A's starts at 0, group B's at 12.
How many steps each leg of the script lasts (indexed like fan_moves); $FF sends a flier back to the start of the script.
Each flier's steps left in its leg, or, while waiting, before it enters.
The waits before each of the six fliers in a group enters, so they come in one behind another.
Cleared at the start of move_fans; nothing reads it.
Where each flier is in the script.
The leg each flier starts on: 0 for group A, 12 for group B.
Column step for each direction of the script.
Each flier's animation counter; its low two bits pick the shape.
Row step for each direction.
The four first characters of a flier's animation; each shape is four characters from there, two by two.
Toggles which group move_fans moves, so each moves every second call.
Counts the six fliers of the group being moved.
The column each flier enters at.
The entry columns as reset_fans_a copies them.
The row each flier enters at.
The entry rows as reset_fans_a copies them.
0 for the fliers of group A, 1 for group B.
How many of each group's six have been shot; the sixth leaves a capsule.
The Vic Viper's screen row, for the fliers' turn toward it.

Moves one group of six character-drawn fliers (the two groups take turns). A waiting flier counts down and enters at its start cell. A flying one erases its four cells, keeping two of the characters it covered so a laser there can be seen (fan_lasered), follows its script one cell a step, turns at the Vic Viper's row when it reaches the leg that waits for it, and is drawn again as four animated characters in colour 14. One that leaves the playfield is freed.
Looks for one of the twelve shot and missile slots within a cell of cell_x, cell_y (same row or the one below, same column or the one to the right). Returns the slot in A, or $FF if none. Keeps X.
Holds X across shot_at.

An enemy has been destroyed at cell_x, cell_y: scores 100 unless the ship is exploding, and starts an explosion there in a free explosion slot (after clearing the oldest with explosions_reset when none is free). The explosion keeps the four characters it covers that are background (from $27 to $7F) so it can put them back.
Holds X across enemy_destroyed.
Holds Y across enemy_destroyed.
Reads the character at offset Y from the cell: returns it if it is background ($27-$7F, below scenery_limit), or a space if it is anything else.
Explosions, the character each one covers at its top left.
The character each covers at its bottom left.
The character each covers at its top right.
The character each covers at its bottom right.
Puts group A's six fliers (slots 0-5) back waiting at their entry cells with their delays and first leg.
The same for group B (slots 6-11).
Counts formations launched; its low bit picks the group.
Formations launched this stage; at 10 no more come. $0B (more than 10) stops them altogether.
The two characters move_fans found under a flier's right-hand cells.
Every 140 frames sends the next formation of six fliers, group A and group B by turns, until ten have come.
Returns non-zero, and destroys the flier, if either character it covered was part of a laser beam ($5B-$63).

Destroys flier X: erases its four cells, counts the kill in its group (the sixth kill of a group makes its explosion leave a capsule), calls enemy_destroyed, frees the slot and plays sound 4. Returns 1.
Holds X across kill_fan.
Tests each flying flier against the Vic Viper's shots and missiles; one that is hit loses its shot and is destroyed.
Explosions, up to four (explosion_slots): each one's column.
Each one's row.
Frames left in each explosion, 11 down to 1; 0 when free.
For each frame of an explosion (indexed by boom_time), the first of the four characters drawn, two by two: $58, $54, $50 and $4C as it fades.
The character move_explosions draws at the top left.
At the top right.
At the bottom left.
At the bottom right.
Set for an explosion that leaves a capsule when it ends.
The colour of each frame of an explosion, flickering between red, yellow and white.
The colour move_explosions paints this frame.
Draws each explosion's next frame: four characters and their colours, counting down. On the last frame it puts back the four background characters it covered, and drops a capsule if it was marked to.
The loop step of move_explosions.

The blue capsule's power, destroying the enemies on screen. Every sprite enemy in slots 1-6 that is not already exploding, not a big sprite and not off the right edge is destroyed where it stands (a red one, colour 2, leaves a capsule); so are the three objects at $61CB, the six at $7067 and every flier that has entered. Then the background flashes white and fades (bg_flash) and sound 5 plays.
How many explosion slots enemy_destroyed searches: 4.
When no explosion slot is free: drops the capsule if one was due, otherwise blanks the 2x2 cells at once.
Which of the six heads head_fire looks at this call; it goes round all six.

Fifth-stage heads (the stage whose routine is $6DC8), six slots: a head that has scrolled past column 38 is freed; one whose mouth timer is running counts it down, and below 60 fires a ring from its mouth (fire_ring). Every 5 to 14 calls a random head whose timer is idle is set to open its mouth (timer 8).
Calls until head_fire next picks a head to open its mouth.
Screen offsets of the four cells, one under another, that head_hits tests.

Tests the column two to the left of each head on four rows for one of the Vic Viper's shots or missiles ($28-$2A) or a laser ($5B-$63). Each hit takes one from the head's strength and makes a small explosion; at 0 the head is erased (all 24 of its cells), scores 1200, plays sound 5 and leaves a capsule.
Holds X across head_hits.
The screen offsets of a head's 24 cells, six across and four down.

Code that nothing calls: two calls to the sound routines, then a game start for one player that zeroes the score, gives three lives and runs the stage from the byte at $5F97. It looks like the one-player game loop that game_loop replaced.
The lives of the player now playing.
Draws up to three Vic Viper icons (characters $21 and $22) at the top left of the screen, one per life.
Icons still to draw.
Set to 11 by stage_setup; title_stars draws stars only while it is non-zero.
Each stage's first shared multicolour ($D022).
Each stage's second shared multicolour ($D023).
Each stage's value for $924A, read by the enemy-fire routine.
Each stage's value for $9049, and half of it for $904A.
Each stage's value for $8FC1.
Each stage's value for $924B.
Each stage's value for $8FC0.
Each stage's scenery_limit, put back by reset_stage_limit.

Sets up the current stage: clears the screen, keeps the stage number to 0-7, takes its two shared colours, the rate tables and the start of its map, paints colour RAM row by row from row_colours, switches on multicolour, points the video chip at the screen at $0400 and characters at $3800, sets the sprite colours, and zeroes the tables of enemies, shots and options.
Non-zero while the title runs: stage_setup clears it, and title_stars then does not twinkle.
For each of the three hatch-like objects, the rows below its top at which it fires.
Three character-drawn objects that fire rings: each one's column.
Each one's row; 0 when free.
The first character of each object's shape.
Each object's colour; colour 10 marks one that leaves a capsule when the blue capsule destroys it.
Draws the three ring-firing objects, each two by two characters, colouring their cells (hatch_paint); one that leaves columns 1 to 41 is erased and freed.
The six colour-RAM offsets hatch_paint colours, three across on two rows.
The colour hatch_paint uses.
Colours six cells of an object in its colour.
Picks one of the three objects at random and, if it is there, fires a ring from three columns to its right at its firing row (fire_ring).

Moves the twelve stars of the title's star field left by each one's speed, erasing each at its old cell and drawing it at the new one; a star that leaves the screen comes back at the right on a random row with a random speed. In play (when the flag at $633E is set) it only twinkles the background stars (twinkle).
Set when the stage's scenery has run out and the boss is due: the title's star field takes over the background, and boss_phase runs.

The raster interrupt's body. Acknowledges the video chip, keeps $FB-$FE and cell_x/cell_y for the main program, and steps a counter through four phases, one per interrupt, each setting the line for the next: phase 0 at line 40 turns extended colour off and draws the sprites; phase 1 at line 71 sets the playfield's colours and fine scroll; phase 2 at line 80 runs the game's movers; phase 3, asked for at line 224 but taken only when phase 2 has finished, sets the power-up bar's colours and extended colour and steps the scroll (scroll_step). Ends at irq_exit.
The colours a flash fades through, read backwards from bg_flash: white, yellow, light grey, grey, dark grey and black, with the stage's background first.
Frames left in a background flash; each frame takes the next colour from flash_colours into bg_colour.
Phase 3 of irq_chain: blacks the background, turns on extended colour for the bar at the bottom, steps the scroll, and asks for line 40 for phase 0.
Phase 0 of irq_chain: turns extended colour off, blacks the border, draws the sprites, plays queued sound, and asks for line 71 for phase 1.

Phase 2 of irq_chain: moves the ship (or, while it explodes, the explosion), then the enemies, shots and effects. Odd and even frames share the work: one half runs one set of movers, the other half the rest.
Counts interrupts; its low two bits pick the phase of irq_chain.
The playfield's fine horizontal scroll, 7 down to 0; it wraps from 0 back to 7 when the map moves a whole character.
Counts phase-2 interrupts, so once a frame; its low bit splits the movers between frames.

Every second frame steps scroll_x down a pixel. At 6 it shifts the map a character (map_shift); at 7 it draws the new column (map_column) and sets the flag at $6D44. On the other frames it runs the stage's own routine from stage_routines. On the title it only runs title_tick.
Set when scroll_step has shifted the map, cleared in phase 3; phase 0 then runs the work at $7307.
The routine each stage runs every second frame (by stage, two bytes each): the enemy waves and the stage's own objects.

The main program's loop during a stage: steps the ship's controls, the player's shots and the power-up bar, then the collision and pause tail. Leaves when the stage is cleared (stage_cleared), or when the ship has been hit and no shield is left (the death sequence starts), or when the game ends.
Set when the turn ends; game_loop then stops at once.
Set when the stage's boss is beaten; the play loop then moves to the next stage, after stage 8 back to stage 1 with the ending (ending).
Puts the KERNAL's IRQ address back in $0314 and turns off the raster interrupt.
The sprite collision register as check_collisions read it.

Reads the video chip's sprite collision register. When the ship's sprite (bit 0) has touched another, finds each slot in use that collided and lies within 12 of the ship's X (in two-pixel units) and 21 of its Y, and on the first: sets ship_hit and plays sound 5. A slot that is a big sprite (spr_big) empties the shield count instead; any other slot is switched off.
The bit mask of each sprite slot, for testing collision_bits.
Puts back $FB-$FE and cell_x/cell_y as the main program left them, then returns into irq.
Where irq_chain keeps $FB-$FE.

The stage's end, once the scenery has run out (boss_mode): counts down, clears the remaining enemies, then builds the Big Core and each frame runs its movement, lasers, timer and hits. When its five walls are gone it scores 500 and the stage is cleared; when its timer (core_time) runs out first, the stage is cleared without the points.
Low bytes of each stage's character block, eight stages.
High bytes of each stage's character block.

Copies the current stage's 1 KB of characters to $3C00, the top half of the character set at $3800, from the address in stage_charset_lo/hi; then loads the stage's 512 bytes at $8000 and its colour row.
Low bytes of each stage's 512-byte block for $8000.
High bytes of the same.
Copies 512 bytes for the current stage from stage_block_lo/hi to $8000, then the stage's colours (load_stage_colours).
Low bytes of each stage's 25 row colours.
High bytes of the same.
Copies the current stage's 25 colour bytes, one per screen row, to row_colours ($41CB).
Frames left in the current 50 for core_clock.
Called each frame of the boss: every 50 frames takes one from core_time.
Counts down once every 50 frames (core_clock) while the Big Core is on screen; at 0 the core leaves and the stage ends without its points.
The raster interrupt's entry. Saves the registers, runs irq_chain, acknowledges CIA 1, and returns.
Marks sprite slot 0 (the ship) in use, then tests the fliers against the shots.
